synopsis: Cluttered off-road environments create both missed-detection and unnecessary-braking risks: idealized perception cannot establish that radar resolves a worker beside a large metal structure, while operational triggers include rock piles, berms, adjacent machines and the truck’s own tyres [f2578, f3022, f4362]. Radar is considered most likely to remain useful in dust and darkness, but radar and ultrasonic simulation of off-road clutter remains low credibility until correlated with the company’s own measurements [f12650, f12774]. The strongest direct off-road radar evidence is the 2025 wheel-loader study, whose synthetic results required hand-built geometry and tuned materials yet still missed real double reflections; validated simulation of piles, highwalls, large steel structures and machine self-reflection was not found for any sensor [f4714, f4422, f12768, f4718]. Real site captures preserve geometry, clutter and unexpected correlations, although photogrammetry itself can fail on textureless soil, glare, reflections and moving objects [f3701, f3753, f4203]. Planning should therefore pair high-value simulated phenomena with physical reference tests before prototype arrival and retain physical testing for unresolved effects within the four-month validation window, rather than treating bench stimulation as realistic reproduction of terrain clutter or steel-structure multipath [f7374, f12751, f5327].
